title: Stacie Mintz – Turning Qualitative Fundamentals into Quantitative Factors (S7E33)

reader_summary.headline: Pimco explains how they turn qualitative insights into quantitative investment factors.
reader_summary.overview: Pimco started its quantitative equity strategy after a client challenged them to beat simple index funds. The team built custom risk models to avoid unfairly punishing growth stocks and focused on unique quality factors. They now test new ideas annually and use fewer, carefully chosen signals to understand what drives performance.

key_points.text: Pimco built a custom risk model in 1999 because standard models unfairly punished growth stocks they wanted to hold.
key_points.evidence_quote: We realized that your portfolio is really the combination of obviously your alpha model and your risk model, and the risk model really was having a big influence on the portfolio. And specifically, we had insights that we were trying to get into the portfolio, and some of those insights, the risk model saw as a risk and would unwind them.

key_points.text: The firm focuses on unique quality factors instead of common trends to stay different from competitors.
key_points.evidence_quote: So we took that opportunity to really focus on how to be differentiated using alternative data sources, looking beyond these simple factors that look at the biases like momentum or PE. We invested a lot in determining what a quality of a company looked like.

key_points.text: They only add new factors if they understand exactly why the factor works and how it fits with other parts of their model.
key_points.evidence_quote: We want to understand why it works. That will solidify that we think that this is a good factor, we understand why it works, we understand when it works in different market cycles.

key_points.text: The team now accepts shorter data histories for new factors and uses them at lower weights until they understand them better.
key_points.evidence_quote: So it used to be, we wanted to see 20 years of data so that we can see how a factor did through time peaks and valleys, but now we might have information that maybe only goes back five or six or seven years and we just really need to understand that factor better

key_points.text: They start research with simple ideas before using complex tools like large language models to manage risks effectively.
key_points.evidence_quote: So typically the simplest approach is really the best approach and so we want to start with something more basic and then get increasingly more complex to understand where the sweet spot is. So don't just jump in and use LLMs through your whole model
